summary: Tampere's city board approved a new parking policy running to 2040 on 15 June 2026, which plans progressive street pricing (price rising with parking duration) in the busiest central streets, tighter time limits and a pilot before any permanent change, while steering long stays into car parks. Street parking is split into three paid zones (3.50, 2.20 and 1.40 euros per hour, after a roughly 10 percent rise proposed in December 2024), with more than 4,000 paid street spaces, resident permits at 25 euros a month in most areas, and about 58,600 parking charges issued in 2025. Car parks are dominated by the city-owned Finnpark group, which runs 16 halls in the centre including P-Hämppi (972 spaces under Hämeenkatu, 35 euros daily maximum, a 50 percent Sunday pilot in October and November 2026), alongside Aimo Park, EuroPark and others. The city's central strategy is to move parking underground: a first P-Hämppi extension and the Viinikankatu underground access road are in design and early works, continuing into the 2030s. Park-and-ride is free and under pressure, with Hiedanranta (tram line 1) regularly full on weekday mornings before an extension from 130 to 220 spaces, while the tram network keeps growing towards Pirkkala, Ruotula and, possibly by 2036, Ylöjärvi.

items.text: The city board approved the parking policy to 2040 on 15 June 2026, per Yle. It outlines progressive street pricing in the busiest central shopping streets (price rising with duration, with a recommended street price reaching the underground price at 30 minutes), stricter time limits, and a pilot before any permanent decision; a later occupancy-based variable price that could replace the zones is only mentioned as a possibility.
items.source_title: Tampere suunnittelee uudenlaista mallia pysäköintiin: hinta nousee, mitä kauemmin pysäköi (Yle)

items.text: The city's payment-zone page (updated 16 September 2026) lists three street zones: zone 1 at 3.50 euros/hour with a 2-hour limit, zone 2 at 2.20 euros/hour with 4 hours, and zone 3 at 1.40 euros/hour with 10 hours. Zone 1 costs half on Sundays and public holidays, zones 2 and 3 are free then, and paid street parking also exists in Hervanta and Kaupi.

In December 2024 Yle reported a city proposal to raise street parking prices by about 10 percent from 1 February (zone 1 from 3.20 to 3.50 euros, zone 2 from 2.00 to 2.20, zone 3 from 1.20 to 1.40), the first rise since 2019. The same article quotes the deputy mayor saying there were no plans for a parking discount for electric cars, unlike Helsinki and Espoo, with a review in a couple of years; the rates now on the city's price page match the proposal.
items.source_title: Tampere ei aio keventää sähköautoilijoiden parkkimaksuja, vaikka Helsinki ja Espoo niin jo tekevät (Yle)

items.text: Resident permits in zones A-K cost 25 euros a month or 300 euros a year (zone L 12.50 euros a month), guest permits 5 euros a day, and the commuter permit in zones F, G, H, J, K 56 euros a month (28 in L). The page (updated 2 June 2026) also lists a 75 percent resident-permit discount for fully electric cars and 50 percent for others if the car is in a peer-to-peer rental service.

The parking policy compares resident and business permits issued in January 2024 with street spaces per zone: zones A and D were fully used (101 and 100 percent), zone J 52 percent, zone K 32 percent and zone L only 7 percent. It also says the permit zones are fragmented and cheaper than in other large Finnish cities, and that the system should be reviewed as underground parking grows.

The city's enforcement statistics (updated 13 February 2026) show 58,649 parking charges in 2025, down from 68,774 in 2023, worth 4.6 million euros, with 17 enforcement staff. The city states it has over 4,000 paid street parking spaces, with payment machines run by Finnpark.

The policy's 2022 parking survey found 41,750 car spaces in the central study area (up 4 percent since 2018), including 6,600 public street and surface-lot spaces and 18 car parks with 8,150 spaces. Street and surface-lot spaces fell 7 percent while public car park capacity rose 20 percent, and about 58 percent of households in the area have no car.

The city's parking-places page (updated 23 February 2026) points to car park operators Aimo Park, EuroPark, Finnpark, Pyynikin Trikoon parkki and Sokos, and says the list is not complete. Street parking can be paid by cash, card or the Moovy, ParkMan, EasyPark, eParking and Flowbird apps, and not every meter still accepts cash.

The Finnpark page for P-Hämppi, read on 21 October 2026, lists 972 spaces and a weekday tariff of 4.20 euros/hour for the first 3 hours (7-23), 3.00 euros/hour after that and 0.50 euros/hour at night, with a 35 euro daily maximum. A 24/7 contract costs 250 euros a month and the resident contract 150 euros a month.

Finnpark announced a two-month pilot with Sunday parking in P-Hämppi at half price in October and November 2026: 2.10 euros/hour for the first three hours, 1.50 euros/hour afterwards and 0.25 euros/hour at night. It said this follows customer wishes on pricing and matches the 50 percent Sunday level on city streets.
items.source_title: Sunnuntait puoleen hintaan P-Hämpissä loka-marraskuun ajan (Finnpark)

items.text: Finnpark extended its resident parking in September 2026 from five to nine central halls (adding P-Hämppi, P-Plevna, P-Koskenparkki and P-Pellavanparkki) for residents of postcodes 33100, 33200 and 33210 without their own space. It says demand is strongest in P-Hämeenpuisto and P-Näsinkulma in the older western centre.

A Finnpark survey of 3,587 Moovy app users in July 2026 found 90 percent fairly or very satisfied with its halls, while pricing, signage and space availability and size were the main requests. Finnpark, a city-owned group running over 30 facilities and some 20,000 spaces in Finland (2025 revenue 31.7 million euros), said it is converting three spaces into two in older halls such as P-Tullintori and P-Asema.
items.source_title: Finnpark tutki: näin tamperelaiset autoilijat kokevat keskustan pysäköinnin (Finnpark)

items.text: The Finnpark P-Hämppi page, read on 21 October 2026, lists 39 charging points on level P1 (35 Type 2 at 22 kW and 4 CCS at 180 kW), operated by Plugit, at 0.33 euros/kWh by day and 0.22 at night for the 22 kW points. The city policy puts plug-in cars at about 10 percent of Tampere's roughly 100,000 cars at the end of 2023.

In February 2026 a team of Finnmap Infra, Sitowise and Ramboll was chosen to design the Viinikankatu underground access road and the first P-Hämppi extension, a joint procurement of the city and Finnpark Parkisto. The project is long-running and continues into the 2030s, with the extension to be built under Rautatienkatu and the current P-Asema.
items.source_title: Tampere jatkaa keskusta-alueen kehittämistä - suunnitteluryhmä valittu (Finnpark)

items.text: The city's page on underground parking (updated 12 May 2026) says the aim is to move street-level capacity phase by phase into underground facilities, with the Viinikankatu connection built together with the first P-Hämppi extension. It reports that construction of the Yliopistontunneli access tunnel started in May and the Viinikankatu section will take about two years before tunnel excavation.
items.source_title: Underground parking and driving connections in the city centre (Tampere)

items.text: Yle reported that Hiedanranta, Tampere's largest park-and-ride at tram line 1, has 130 spaces that were nearly full by 9 a.m. on two of three observed weekday mornings. The city promised 90 more spaces (to 220) by autumn 2026, said there were no plans to charge, and Yle noted 16 park-and-ride sites across Tampere and neighbouring municipalities.
items.source_title: Tampereen suosituimmassa liityntäparkissa ruudut loppuvat kesken (Yle)

items.text: Nysse's park-and-ride page, read on 21 October 2026, lists Hiedanranta with 220 car spaces (12-hour limit), Niihama 70, Kaukajärvi 58 and Koivistonkylä 34, and says workday parking is free. Real-time free-space data for Niihama is shown in the Nysse journey planner and on iot.tampere.fi (Finnish only).

Tram line 1 was extended to Lentävänniemi on 7 January 2025; the tram began in August 2021 and made 16.6 million trips in 2024, with a 24 km network. Extensions to Pirkkala and, via TAYS, to Ruotula and later Linnainmaa were under construction from December 2024.
items.source_title: Tampereen uusin ratikkalinja on valmis - kävimme koeajelulla (Yle)

gaps: WebSearch budget ran out during the task: Aamulehti, Tamperelainen and Nysse news items were not found or opened, so there is no press coverage of centre traffic changes, pedestrianisation or closures beyond Yle.
No occupancy or utilisation statistics for car parks (Finnpark halls, P-Hämppi) or street parking were found; only permit-zone usage (January 2024) and anecdotal park-and-ride fullness.

The completion of the Hiedanranta park-and-ride extension to 220 spaces was not confirmed with a dated source (Nysse's undated page lists 220; the Yle article of March 2026 only promised it for autumn 2026).
The policy's progressive pricing has no adopted tariff or pilot date; the full 64-page policy was extracted but only the sections on supply, pricing, permits and park-and-ride were read.
Opening dates for the Pirkkala/Ruotula tram extensions and the Lielahti-Ylöjärvi route (Yle, 11 February 2026: possible start 2036, no decision) were not verified from official tram project pages.
No low-emission or access-restriction zone for cars was found for Tampere; the centre's pedestrian-street plans were not researched.
iot.tampere.fi (open parking data) returned an empty page and could not be read.
